newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya bourse dealers fear further losses in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kenya bourse dealers fear further losses in 1997.

text.p: Kenyan stocks may suffer further losses in 1997 because of fears of a surge in government spending ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections, dealers said.
"Our main problem is that we have a lot of speculators in the market. Very few people accept the idea of investing for long-term purposes," a leading market analyst said.
But a continuing flow of new issues may help to boost investor interest, which has switched recently to high-yielding treasury bills.
The last time elections were held in Kenya -- in 1992 -- the government printed money to finance its campaign, leading to a sharp rise in inflation and severe depreciation of the Kenyan shilling.
However, brokers said further initial public offerings in 1997, such as the Booker Tate-managed Mumias Sugar Co and Serena Hotels & Lodges, would help maintain investor interest.
"1997 is going to be a very interesting year to watch," said an executive from leading brokers Shah, Munge & Partners.
"There've been a lot of new initiatives which have received tremendous support in the secondary market," he added. "We expect these to fuel up the index and turn around the market."
But some brokers said market performance, especially in the first quarter, depended on end-year company results.
The total value of new issues rose to 4.542 billion shillings in 1996 from 2.5 billion shillings in 1994. There were no public issues in 1995.
The value of private placements rose to 6.5 billion shillings in 1996 from 102 million in 1995, according to market figures.

Bourse officials said the increase was attributed mainly to a total of 235 million shares the government floated in Kenya Airways at 11.25 shillings each, and introduction of East African Development Bank corporate bonds totalling 600 million shillings.
The Central Bank of Kenya plans to issue next year a total of 5.0 billion shillings of treasury bonds with floating-rate interest linked to 91-day treasury bills.
Trading interest may also be sparked by international investment fund Regent Undervalued Assets Fund which has applied for listing in Nairobi as well as Dublin and Botswana.

Between January and December 13, turnover rose a marginal 6.0 percent over the same period in 1995. Foreign investor transactions rose to 600 million shillings from 195 million, of which 72 million were sales compared to 24 million in 1995, bourse officials said.
The market index opened at 3,468.88 in January 1996, dropped to below 3,000 at end-August and closed Thursday at 3,105.56.
Brokers said the majority of active shares in the market Kenya Commercial Bank, Sasini Tea & Coffee, Kenya Breweries, Kenya Power & Lighting and Rea Vipingo were supported by foreign demand.
The Kenyan market has an average price/earnings ratio of 9.08. "Foreigners find our market cheap to invest in because they think it is undervalued," a bourse official said.
